mean: to accept what one is told without question
lit: to swallow something whole, the way a cormorant gulps down a fish without chewing

use.how: Takes information, claims or rumours as its object with を: 噂を鵜呑みにする. Mostly in warnings and criticism: 鵜呑みにしないで.

near.diff: 真に受ける is taking a joke, pleasantry or casual remark as serious; 鵜呑みにする is accepting information or claims without checking them.

cue: Your friend bought an expensive supplement because an advert promised it cures everything, and never checked anything. What did he do with the advert?

ctx.s: 調[しら]べもせずにネットの情報[じょうほう]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}はいけない。
ctx.en: You mustn't believe what you read online without checking it.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は広告[こうこく]の言葉[ことば]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}、高[たか]いサプリを買[か]ってしまった。
ctx.en: He believed the advert without question and ended up buying expensive supplements.

ctx.s: 「専門家[せんもんか]がそう言[い]ってたよ。」「でも、それを{鵜呑[うの]みにする}のは危[あぶ]ないと思[おも]うな。」
ctx.en: "An expert said so." "Still, I think it's risky to just take that at face value."

ctx.s: 噂[うわさ]を{鵜呑[うの]みにした}社員[しゃいん]たちは、事実[じじつ]を確[たし]かめようともしなかった。
ctx.en: The staff who swallowed the rumour didn't even try to check the facts.

ctx.s: 教科書[きょうかしょ]の説明[せつめい]も{鵜呑[うの]みにせず}、自分[じぶん]で確[たし]かめなさい。
ctx.en: Don't accept even the textbook's explanation blindly; check it for yourself.

ctx.s: 調査結果[ちょうさけっか]を{鵜呑[うの]みにする}前[まえ]に、誰[だれ]が調[しら]べたのかを確認[かくにん]しよう。
ctx.en: Before accepting the survey results as they are, let's check who carried out the survey.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]に教[おし]わった方法[ほうほう]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}、成績[せいせき]が上[あ]がりました。
bad.en: (meant: I followed my teacher's method faithfully and my grades went up)
bad.why: It always implies foolishly accepting without checking, so it cannot praise following good advice.

bad.s: 周[まわ]りに反対[はんたい]されても、彼[かれ]は自分[じぶん]の夢[ゆめ]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}頑張[がんば]った。
bad.en: (meant: he kept believing in his dream despite opposition)
bad.why: It is about uncritically accepting what others tell you, not about faith or conviction in your own goals.

mean: to take at face value what was not meant seriously
lit: to receive words as truth (ma), as if they had been meant in earnest

use.how: Takes a joke, pleasantry, flattery or offhand remark as object with を; very often in 真に受けないで. The speaker implies the words were not meant seriously.

near.diff: 鵜呑みにする is accepting information or claims without checking; 真に受ける is taking a joke or polite remark as if it were meant seriously.

cue: A neighbour said "Drop by anytime!" just to be polite, and you actually turned up at their door on Sunday. What did you do with the remark?

ctx.s: 冗談[じょうだん]だよ。{真[ま]に受[う]けない}で。
ctx.en: I'm only joking. Don't take it seriously.

ctx.s: 「今度[こんど]遊[あそ]びに来[き]てね」という社交辞令[しゃこうじれい]を{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、本当[ほんとう]に行[い]ってしまった。
ctx.en: I took "come and visit sometime" literally, though it was only politeness, and actually went.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]は「天才[てんさい]だね」と言[い]われたのを{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、すっかりその気[き]になっている。
ctx.en: My little brother believed it when someone called him a genius, and now he's completely full of himself.

ctx.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]、明日[あした]は休[やす]んでいいって言[い]ってたよね？」「まさか、あれを{真[ま]に受[う]けた}の？」
ctx.en: "The manager said we could take tomorrow off, right?" "Don't tell me you took that seriously."

ctx.s: 酔[よ]った勢[いきお]いでした約束[やくそく]なんて、{真[ま]に受[う]ける}人[ひと]はいないよ。
ctx.en: Nobody takes a promise made while drunk seriously.

ctx.s: エイプリルフールの記事[きじ]を{真[ま]に受[う]けた}読者[どくしゃ]から、問[と]い合[あ]わせが相次[あいつ]いだ。
ctx.en: Readers who believed the April Fools' article sent in one enquiry after another.

bad.s: 医者[いしゃ]の説明[せつめい]を{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、毎日[まいにち]薬[くすり]を飲[の]んでいる。
bad.en: (meant: I followed the doctor's advice and take my medicine every day)
bad.why: It implies the words were not meant seriously; for serious advice you simply believe or follow it.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は仕事[しごと]を{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、毎晩[まいばん]遅[おそ]くまで働[はたら]いている。
bad.en: (meant: he takes his job seriously and works late every night)
bad.why: Its object is something someone said, not a task; taking one's work seriously is a different expression.

mean: to accept someone's kind offer gratefully
lit: to lean on someone's kind words, the way a child leans on an indulgent parent

use.how: Said politely to the person who made the offer, usually after being urged: では、お言葉に甘えて. Common in speech and business email.

cue: Your host insists you leave the washing-up and go and rest. You decline once, they insist again, and you accept. What do you say?

ctx.s: 「どうぞ座[すわ]ってください。」「では、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}。」
ctx.en: "Please, have a seat." "Well then, thank you, I will."

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]はもう帰[かえ]っていいよ。」「すみません、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}お先[さき]に失礼[しつれい]します。」
ctx.en: "You can go home now." "Thank you, then I'll take you up on that and head off."

ctx.s: 「遠慮[えんりょ]しないで、たくさん食[た]べてね。」「ありがとうございます。{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えさせて}いただきます。」
ctx.en: "Don't hold back, eat as much as you like." "Thank you, I'll gladly accept."

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]が駅[えき]まで車[くるま]で送[おく]ると言[い]ってくれたので、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]える}ことにした。
ctx.en: My senior colleague offered to drive me to the station, so I decided to accept.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]か断[ことわ]ったが、おばあさんが譲[ゆず]らないので、最後[さいご]は{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えた}。
ctx.en: I said no several times, but the old lady wouldn't take no for an answer, so in the end I accepted her kindness.

ctx.s: 締[し]め切[き]りを延[の]ばしていただけるとのこと、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}来週[らいしゅう]提出[ていしゅつ]いたします。
ctx.en: Since you kindly offered to extend the deadline, I will gratefully take you up on it and submit next week.

bad.s: 店員[てんいん]に{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}、お水[みず]をくださいと頼[たの]んだ。
bad.en: (meant: I politely asked the waiter for some water)
bad.why: It accepts an offer someone else has made; it cannot introduce a request of your own.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]に褒[ほ]められて、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}とてもうれしかった。
bad.en: (meant: my teacher praised me and I was delighted)
bad.why: It is about accepting an offer of help or a favour, not about enjoying a compliment.

mean: to be a good judge of people or things
lit: to have eyes that see: eyes that can tell what is good from what is not

use.how: Predicate about a person, often with what is judged: 人を見る目がある. The negative 見る目がない criticises poor judgment.

near.diff: 甘いものに目がない means being crazy about something; only 見る目がない, the negative of this idiom, means poor judgment.

cue: Every person your manager has ever hired has turned out to be excellent. What can you say about her?

ctx.s: この絵[え]を選[えら]ぶなんて、君[きみ]は{見[み]る目[め]がある}ね。
ctx.en: You picked this painting? You've got a good eye.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は人[ひと]を{見[み]る目[め]がある}から、彼女[かのじょ]が採用[さいよう]した人[ひと]はみんな優秀[ゆうしゅう]だ。
ctx.en: She's a good judge of people, so everyone she hires turns out to be excellent.

ctx.s: 部下[ぶか]を{見[み]る目[め]がない}上司[じょうし]の下[もと]では、優秀[ゆうしゅう]な人[ひと]ほど辞[や]めていく。
ctx.en: Under a boss who can't judge his staff, the best people are the first to leave.

ctx.s: あんな人[ひと]と付[つ]き合[あ]うなんて、私[わたし]は人[ひと]を{見[み]る目[め]がなかった}。
ctx.en: Going out with someone like that... I was a poor judge of character.

ctx.s: 骨董品[こっとうひん]の世界[せかい]では、本物[ほんもの]を{見[み]る目[め]がある}かどうかがすべてだ。
ctx.en: In the antiques trade, everything depends on whether you can tell the genuine article.

ctx.s: 無名[むめい]だった頃[ころ]の彼[かれ]を見[み]つけたスカウトは、さすがに{見[み]る目[め]があった}。
ctx.en: The scout who discovered him back when he was unknown certainly knew talent when he saw it.

bad.s: 祖父[そふ]は八十歳[はちじゅっさい]だが、まだ{見[み]る目[め]がある}ので眼鏡[めがね]はいらない。
bad.en: (meant: my grandfather is eighty but his eyesight is still good)
bad.why: It is about judgment and taste, not about eyesight.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は甘[あま]いものに{見[み]る目[め]がある}ので、毎日[まいにち]ケーキを食[た]べている。
bad.en: (meant: he loves sweets, so he eats cake every day)
bad.why: Loving something is the different idiom me ga nai; this one praises good judgment.

mean: to encourage someone to take the plunge
lit: to push someone gently on the back so they take the step forward

use.how: Object is a person hesitating over a step they want to take: 友達の背中を押す. Often てくれた, or passive 背中を押された. A word or event can also be the subject.

near.diff: 一肌脱ぐ is stepping in to do real work to help someone; 背中を押す is giving the encouragement that lets them act for themselves.

cue: You were unsure about applying to study abroad until a teacher told you to go for it, and so you did. What did the teacher do for you?

ctx.s: 迷[まよ]っていた私[わたし]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}くれたのは、母[はは]の一言[ひとこと]だった。
ctx.en: What gave me the push I needed when I was hesitating was something my mother said.

ctx.s: 「転職[てんしょく]、まだ迷[まよ]ってるの？」「うん、誰[だれ]かに{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}ほしいんだ。」
ctx.en: "Still unsure about changing jobs?" "Yeah, I want someone to give me a push."

ctx.s: 留学[りゅうがく]するか悩[なや]んでいる友達[ともだち]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}あげたい。
ctx.en: I want to encourage my friend, who can't decide whether to study abroad.

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]が夢[ゆめ]を叶[かな]えたのを見[み]て、{背中[せなか]を押[お]された}気[き]がした。
ctx.en: Seeing my senior make her dream come true felt like a push to go for mine.

ctx.s: この本[ほん]は、新[あたら]しいことを始[はじ]めたい人[ひと]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}くれる。
ctx.en: This book gives encouragement to people who want to start something new.

ctx.s: 低金利[ていきんり]が、家[いえ]の購入[こうにゅう]を考[かんが]える人[ひと]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}いる。
ctx.en: Low interest rates are encouraging people who are thinking of buying a home.

bad.s: 母[はは]は毎朝[まいあさ]、宿題[しゅくだい]をしなさいと私[わたし]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]す}。
bad.en: (meant: my mother nags me every morning to do my homework)
bad.why: It is encouragement toward a step the person wants to take, not nagging about chores.

bad.s: 上司[じょうし]は嫌[いや]がる部下[ぶか]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}、無理[むり]やり契約[けいやく]させた。
bad.en: (meant: the boss forced his unwilling subordinate to sign)
bad.why: It is supportive encouragement of someone's own wish, never pressure that forces a person against their will.

lit: to put fighting spirit into oneself, as with a shout before a bout

use.how: Of oneself before an effort: 気合を入れていこう. As 気合を入れて + verb, doing something with extra energy; or someone rallies others: 選手に気合を入れる.

near.diff: 本腰を入れる is getting seriously committed to a task over time; 気合を入れる is summoning energy for the effort right in front of you.
気を引き締める is becoming alert and careful so as not to slip up; 気合を入れる is firing up energy and spirit.

cue: Just before the final, the captain slaps his own cheeks and shouts to fire himself up. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 明日[あした]は決勝[けっしょう]だ。大[おお]きな声[こえ]を出[だ]して、{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}いこう！
ctx.en: The final is tomorrow. Let's shout it out and get fired up!

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は両手[りょうて]で頬[ほお]を叩[たた]いて{気合[きあい]を入[い]れた}。
ctx.en: He slapped his cheeks with both hands to psych himself up.

ctx.s: 「その服[ふく]、すごいね。」「今日[きょう]はデートだから、ちょっと{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}きたんだ。」
ctx.en: "Wow, look at that outfit." "I've got a date today, so I made a bit of an effort."

ctx.s: 「よし、やるぞ！」と{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}、大掃除[おおそうじ]に取[と]りかかった。
ctx.en: Saying "Right, let's do this!", I psyched myself up and got stuck into the big clean.

ctx.s: 朝[あさ]は苦手[にがて]なので、濃[こ]いコーヒーで{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}から仕事[しごと]を始[はじ]める。
ctx.en: I'm not a morning person, so I fire myself up with strong coffee before starting work.

ctx.s: 負[ま]けている選手[せんしゅ]たちに、監督[かんとく]が大声[おおごえ]で{気合[きあい]を入[い]れた}。
ctx.en: The coach roared at his losing players to fire them up.

bad.s: 疲[つか]れたので、ソファに寝転[ねころ]んで{気合[きあい]を入[い]れた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was tired, so I lay on the sofa to recharge)
bad.why: It means summoning energy and fighting spirit for an effort, not resting or relaxing.

bad.s: 道[みち]が凍[こお]っているから、{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}ゆっくり歩[ある]こう。
bad.en: (meant: the road is icy, so let's walk slowly and carefully)
bad.why: It is about energy and drive; being careful and cautious is ki o tsukeru, not this.

mean: to feel that one's effort is getting results
lit: to feel a response come back into one's hand, as when a fish takes the line

use.how: Said by the person who made the effort, about an exam, interview, project or attempt: 試験は手応えがあった. 手応えがない means no sign of results.

near.diff: 軌道に乗る says a project is actually running smoothly; 手応えがある is the felt sense that one's effort is working.

cue: Walking out of a job interview, you feel your answers landed and it went well. How do you describe the interview to a friend?

ctx.s: 今日[きょう]の試験[しけん]は{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
ctx.en: I feel today's exam went well.

ctx.s: 「面接[めんせつ]どうだった？」「うん、けっこう{手応[てごた]えがあった}よ。」
ctx.en: "How was the interview?" "Yeah, I think it went pretty well."

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい教[おし]え方[かた]を試[ため]してみたら、生徒[せいと]たちの目[め]が輝[かがや]き、{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
ctx.en: When I tried a new way of teaching, the students' eyes lit up and I felt it was working.

ctx.s: 説明会[せつめいかい]は質問[しつもん]もたくさん出[で]て、{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
ctx.en: Lots of questions came up at the information session, so I felt it really worked.

ctx.s: いくら練習[れんしゅう]しても{手応[てごた]えがない}ので、やり方[かた]を変[か]えてみた。
ctx.en: However much I practised I wasn't getting anywhere, so I tried changing my approach.

ctx.s: 営業[えいぎょう]を始[はじ]めて半年[はんとし]、ようやく{手応[てごた]えがある}と感[かん]じられるようになった。
ctx.en: Six months into the sales job, I'm finally starting to feel my efforts are paying off.

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たって、{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
bad.en: (meant: I won the lottery and felt lucky)
bad.why: It is the felt sense that one's own effort is working; a lucky win involves no effort that could pay off.

bad.s: このステーキは肉[にく]が厚[あつ]くて、{手応[てごた]えがある}ね。
bad.en: (meant: this steak is thick and nicely chewy)
bad.why: Chewiness is hagotae; this idiom is about feeling that an effort is producing results.

mean: to flatter, to butter someone up
lit: to grind sesame seeds in a mortar

use.how: The person flattered takes に: 上司にごまをする. Criticises insincere flattery for gain; said of oneself it is joking. Noun: ごますり.

near.diff: 顔色をうかがう is anxiously watching someone's mood; ごまをする is actively flattering them to gain something.

cue: A coworker laughs at all the boss's jokes and praises his taste in ties, hoping for a promotion. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はいつも部長[ぶちょう]に{ごまをすって}いる。
ctx.en: He's always buttering up the department head.

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]は優[やさ]しいね。何[なに]か欲[ほ]しいの？」「ばれた？ちょっと{ごまをすって}みたんだ。」
ctx.en: "You're being sweet today. Want something?" "Busted. I was trying a little flattery."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]に{ごまをすっても}、成績[せいせき]は上[あ]がらないよ。
ctx.en: Sucking up to the teacher won't raise your grades.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はお小遣[こづか]いを増[ふ]やしてもらおうと、父[ちち]に{ごまをすり}始[はじ]めた。
ctx.en: Hoping for a bigger allowance, my little brother started sweet-talking our father.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の前[まえ]でだけ{ごまをする}人[ひと]は、同僚[どうりょう]に信用[しんよう]されない。
ctx.en: People who only flatter when the president is around don't earn their colleagues' trust.

ctx.s: 実力[じつりょく]で認[みと]められたいから、{ごまをする}ようなことはしたくない。
ctx.en: I want to be recognised for my ability, so I don't want to resort to flattery.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]の誕生日[たんじょうび]に、心[こころ]から{ごまをすった}。
bad.en: (meant: I sincerely complimented my friend on her birthday)
bad.why: It always means insincere flattery for one's own gain, never sincere praise.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は上司[じょうし]を{ごまをすって}出世[しゅっせ]した。
bad.en: (meant: he flattered his boss and got promoted)
bad.why: The person flattered takes ni, not o; the o in the idiom already belongs to goma.

mean: to grit one's teeth and endure
lit: to clench one's teeth tightly together

use.how: Mostly as 歯を食いしばって + verb (耐える, 頑張る, 続ける): enduring pain, hardship or frustration and carrying on.

near.diff: 歯が立たない means being no match for an opponent or problem; 歯を食いしばる means enduring hardship and carrying on.

cue: In the last kilometre of a marathon, every step hurts, but you clamp your jaw and refuse to stop. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 痛[いた]かったが、{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}我慢[がまん]した。
ctx.en: It hurt, but I gritted my teeth and bore it.

ctx.s: 「もう走[はし]れない。」「あと少[すこ]しだ、{歯[は]を食[く]いしばれ}！」
ctx.en: "I can't run any more." "Just a bit further, grit your teeth!"

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の頃[ころ]は失敗[しっぱい]ばかりだったが、{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}続[つづ]けてきた。
ctx.en: As a newcomer I failed constantly, but I gritted my teeth and kept at it.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]が亡[な]くなった後[あと]、母[はは]は{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}三人[さんにん]の子[こ]どもを育[そだ]てた。
ctx.en: After my father died, my mother struggled on and raised three children.

ctx.s: 悔[くや]しさに{歯[は]を食[く]いしばる}選手[せんしゅ]の姿[すがた]が、テレビに映[うつ]っていた。
ctx.en: The television showed the player clenching his teeth in frustration.

ctx.s: 苦[くる]しいときこそ{歯[は]を食[く]いしばる}ことが大切[たいせつ]だと、祖父[そふ]はよく言[い]っていた。
ctx.en: My grandfather often said that it is when times are hard that you must grit your teeth and endure.

bad.s: 硬[かた]いおせんべいを{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}食[た]べた。
bad.en: (meant: I crunched my way through a hard rice cracker)
bad.why: It means clenching the teeth to endure, not biting or chewing food.

bad.s: 旅行[りょこう]が楽[たの]しかったので、最後[さいご]まで{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}楽[たの]しんだ。
bad.en: (meant: the trip was fun, so I enjoyed it to the very end)
bad.why: It is only for enduring pain, hardship or frustration, never for enjoying something.

mean: to hit a wall, to run into an obstacle
lit: to walk straight into a wall that blocks the way ahead

use.how: Said of a person or project whose progress stops at an obstacle: 研究が壁にぶつかる. The obstacle can be named: 敬語という壁にぶつかる.

near.diff: 歯が立たない says a particular opponent or problem is beyond you; 壁にぶつかる says progress on a longer path has come to a halt.

cue: After a year of steady progress on the piano, you suddenly can't improve however much you practise. What has happened?

ctx.s: 誰[だれ]でも一度[いちど]は{壁[かべ]にぶつかる}ものだよ。
ctx.en: Everyone hits a wall at some point.

ctx.s: 日本語[にほんご]の勉強[べんきょう]で、敬語[けいご]という{壁[かべ]にぶつかった}。
ctx.en: In my Japanese studies, I ran into the wall of honorific language.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]、仕事[しごと]どう？」「正直[しょうじき]、ちょっと{壁[かべ]にぶつかって}るんだ。」
ctx.en: "How's work lately?" "Honestly, I've kind of hit a wall."

ctx.s: {壁[かべ]にぶつかった}ときこそ、基本[きほん]に戻[もど]るべきだ。
ctx.en: When you hit a wall, that's exactly when you should go back to basics.

ctx.s: 研究[けんきゅう]は資金不足[しきんぶそく]という{壁[かべ]にぶつかり}、中断[ちゅうだん]された。
ctx.en: The research ran into a lack of funding and was put on hold.

ctx.s: 上達[じょうたつ]が止[と]まったと感[かん]じたら、それは{壁[かべ]にぶつかって}いる証拠[しょうこ]かもしれない。
ctx.en: If you feel you've stopped improving, it may be a sign that you've hit a wall.

bad.s: 母[はは]と意見[いけん]が合[あ]わず、夕食[ゆうしょく]の時[とき]に{壁[かべ]にぶつかった}。
bad.en: (meant: my mother and I disagreed and clashed over dinner)
bad.why: It is about progress being blocked by an obstacle, not about quarrelling with a person.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は努力[どりょく]を続[つづ]けて、ついに{壁[かべ]にぶつかった}。
bad.en: (meant: he kept working hard and finally reached his goal)
bad.why: It means getting stuck, not succeeding: even after hard work it describes a setback, never reaching the goal.
